title: The Risen Christ Among the Lampstands
summary: The book opens as a revelation from Jesus Christ, given through an angel to John, with a blessing on those who read, hear, and keep it. John greets the seven churches of Asia in the name of the eternal God, the seven Spirits, and Jesus Christ, and he praises Christ, who loves us and freed us by his blood. On the island of Patmos, on the Lord's day, John sees the glorified Son of Man standing among seven golden lampstands, falls at his feet, and is commissioned to write what he sees.
story: Revelation is the last book of the Bible, and its first chapter introduces its main character and its first audience. Jesus, who in the Gospels was crucified and rose, now appears in heavenly glory, the First and the Last who holds the keys of death. The first readers were seven real churches, some suffering and some compromised, in cities of the Roman province of Asia. This chapter sets up the messages to those churches in chapters 2 and 3, and it sets the tone for everything after: whatever John sees about beasts and empires, it comes from the one who was dead and is alive forever.
historical:
John writes from Patmos, a small, rocky island in the Aegean Sea, southwest of Ephesus and off the coast of what is now Turkey. He says he was there because of the word of God and his testimony about Jesus (verse 9), which most interpreters take to mean that he had been banished for his preaching. Roman authorities used exile to islands as a punishment for people who caused trouble, especially those of some standing. Early tradition holds that John was released and returned to Ephesus.

The date is debated. Most scholars follow Irenaeus, who wrote around AD 180 that John saw the vision near the end of the reign of Domitian, who ruled from AD 81 to 96, placing the book around AD 95. A minority dates it to the late 60s, during or just after the reign of Nero, whose persecution of Christians in Rome followed the great fire of AD 64. Either way, the churches lived under the power of Rome, in cities where the worship of the emperor was woven into civic life. John calls himself a partner with them in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance that are in Jesus (verse 9), three words that summarize the book's message.
cultural:
The seven cities named in verse 11 lay roughly in a circle along a Roman road, in the order a messenger traveling from the coast would reach them, beginning at Ephesus and ending at Laodicea. A letter carried along that route could be read aloud in each church in turn. That is the setting of verse 3's blessing on the one who reads aloud and those who hear: most people could not read, and Scripture was heard in public worship.

The Lord's day (verse 10) is one of the earliest uses of this phrase for the first day of the week, the day of Jesus' resurrection, when Christians gathered to worship. In a world where Roman coins and inscriptions called the emperor lord, the phrase already quietly contests his claim. The imagery of Christ in verses 13-16 draws heavily on the Old Testament: the Son of Man and the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7, the heavenly figure of Daniel 10, the voice like many waters of Ezekiel 43:2. His long robe and golden sash suggest the dress of a priest or a king. Lampstands recall the seven-branched lampstand of the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 25:31-40; Zechariah 4).
literary: Revelation announces three genres in its opening verses. It is an apocalypse (verse 1), a revealing of hidden things through visions, like Daniel. It is a prophecy (verse 3), a word from God calling for a response. And it is a letter (verses 4-5), with sender, recipients, and greeting. The chapter moves from prologue (verses 1-3) to greeting and doxology (verses 4-8), to John's vision and commission (verses 9-20). Numbers carry meaning: seven, the number of completeness, appears repeatedly (seven churches, Spirits, lampstands, stars). The divine name him who is and was and is to come reworks God's name revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14). Verse 7 combines Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10. Verse 19 has been read as an outline of the book: what John has seen, what is, and what will happen after this, though interpreters differ on how neatly it divides the chapters.

outline.t: Prologue: the revelation of Jesus Christ
Greeting and praise to the coming Christ
John on Patmos commanded to write
Vision of the Son of Man among the lampstands
Do not be afraid: the commission explained

doctrines.note: The greeting comes from the eternal God, from the seven Spirits before his throne, and from Jesus Christ (verses 4-5). Many interpreters read the seven Spirits as the Holy Spirit in his fullness, drawing on Isaiah 11:2 and Zechariah 4; others take them as seven angelic beings. Either way, Christ is named alongside God as the source of grace.
Christ loves us and has released us from our sins by his blood (verse 5). His death is the ground of his people's freedom and their calling to be a kingdom of priests.
God is the Alpha and the Omega, the Almighty, the beginning and end of all things. The risen Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades. Nothing the churches face lies outside his rule.
Christ has made his people a kingdom and priests to God (verse 6), language from Exodus 19:6. Believers already share his reign, even while they share in tribulation.

words.note: Apokalypsis, revelation or unveiling, the first word of the book in Greek. It means pulling back a cover to show what was hidden. The book is not a riddle meant to conceal but a disclosure of how things really are, especially who truly rules.

Martys, witness. Jesus is the faithful witness (verse 5), the one who told the truth about God even to death. The word later came to mean martyr, and Revelation is one reason why: faithful witness in this book often costs one's life.

Kyriakos, belonging to the Lord, used in the New Testament only here and of the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 11:20). The Lord's day became the Christian name for Sunday, the day of the resurrection. The adjective was used in the Roman world for things belonging to the emperor, which gives the phrase an edge.

christ: Revelation's first chapter is a portrait of the risen Christ. He is the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth (verse 5), three titles that cover his death, resurrection, and reign. He is coming with the clouds, fulfilling Daniel 7:13, and those who pierced him will see him. He appears as one like the Son of Man, but with features that Daniel gives to the Ancient of Days (hair white like wool), so that he shares God's glory. He takes God's own title, the First and the Last (Isaiah 44:6), and says, I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever. He stands among the churches, holds their angels in his hand, and has authority over death itself. His first word to the terrified John is do not be afraid.

hard.q: The book says these things must soon come to pass and that the time is near. How can that be true two thousand years later?
hard.a:
Verse 1 speaks of what must soon take place, and verse 3 says the time is near. Interpreters have answered the apparent delay in several ways. Preterists argue that much of the book was indeed fulfilled soon, in the events surrounding the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 or the persecution and eventual fall of pagan Rome. Futurists often read soon as meaning suddenly or as describing the next great event on God's calendar, and they point to 2 Peter 3:8, where a day with the Lord is like a thousand years. Idealists and many others read near as a description of the whole age since Christ's resurrection: the last days began with Jesus, and his return is always imminent in the sense that nothing more must happen before it can occur.

What all agree is that the first readers were meant to take the book as urgent. Its message about faithful witness, endurance, and the true ruler of the world concerned their lives immediately, not only a distant future. Each generation since has been addressed the same way.

questions: John describes himself as a partner in tribulation and kingdom and perseverance. How do these three belong together in the Christian life?
The first word the glorified Christ speaks to John is do not be afraid. What fears would change if you saw Jesus as this chapter shows him?
Christ walks among the lampstands, which are the churches. What does it mean for your church that Christ is present in it and knows it?
